finalResponse:
# Lead Time: 14 Weeks, and What It's Actually Made Of

Let me start with the artefact nobody has read.

A certified product leaves behind a date-stamped audit trail — inspection records, material certs, sign-offs, notified-body releases, test reports. Every one of those documents carries a time on it, because that is what certification is *for*. Which means this company has, sitting in its quality archive, a minute-by-minute forensic reconstruction of every unit it has ever shipped, filed by law, indexed, and to my knowledge never once used to answer the question being argued about.

I'd take twenty recently shipped orders — a spread of configurations, not the easy ones — and rebuild each timeline from the dossier. Order receipt to drawing release. Drawing release to first material issue. Each operation. Each gate: time the part arrived at the gate, time the inspector touched it, time the signature landed, time it moved. Then plot the whole thing as a single horizontal bar per order and colour it two ways only: *work* and *waiting*.

I will tell you now roughly what that picture shows, because it shows the same thing in every plant of this type I have looked at, and if it doesn't, that itself is the most interesting finding available and worth the three weeks it takes to get.

Touch time — hands on metal, machine actually cutting, inspector actually inspecting — will come to somewhere between four and nine days. Against a quoted fourteen weeks. Which puts the value-added ratio somewhere around one to two percent, and means the debate between Production, Quality and Sales is a debate about ninety-eight percent of nothing. They are arguing over whose two days to shave.

**So the honest framing is this: nobody is slow. The product is stationary.**

## The distinction the last attempt got wrong, and it cost them two years

Here is what I think happened last time, and it matters more than anything else in this brief.

Someone compressed the schedule by attacking the visible time — the gates, because they're on the routing with a duration written next to them and they look like cost. Inspections were combined, deferred to final, sampled instead of hundred-percented, or run concurrently with downstream operations so that a part moved before it was cleared. Warranty went up. Everyone drew the obvious lesson: *speed causes defects.*

It doesn't. What that programme removed wasn't time. It was **feedback** — the early detection that catches a drifting process at operation four instead of at the customer's site in month nine. Deferring a gate doesn't make the defect later; it makes the *discovery* later, which makes the escape more likely and the rework larger. The programme didn't go fast. It went blind, and then it went fast.

The distinction I'd write on the wall in week one and refuse to let anyone blur:

- **Gate integrity** — what gets checked, to what standard, by whom, with what authority to stop. *Never touched. Not negotiable. Not on the table, not in scope, not in the business case.*
- **Gate latency** — how long a part sits waiting for a gate that takes ninety minutes to perform.

Every hour of the 14 weeks lives in the second category. And I'd expect gate latency alone — waiting for an inspector who covers four cells, batching parts up so a third-party visit is "worth it", the two days a certificate spends in someone's inbox, the nonconformance loop that requires an MRB meeting that convenes on Thursdays — to account for three to five weeks of the fourteen. Without a single inspection being weakened. Some of it goes *away by adding inspection capacity*, which is the sentence that will make Quality an ally rather than a hostage, and which no cost programme in this company's history has ever been allowed to say.

## Where the rest of it is

Four other pools, and each has a different instrument.

**The front end, before anything is made.** Order entry, configuration sign-off, credit, engineering release, procurement raising a PO. Ten to twenty working days is typical, entirely administrative, invisible to Production because Production's clock starts at material issue and invisible to Sales because Sales' clock stops at handshake. Nobody owns it, so nobody measures it, so it is free time to recover — the cheapest weeks in the building.

**Purchased long-lead items.** Castings, forgings, certified pressure parts, controls. If the critical path runs through a 9-week casting, no internal improvement matters and the whole exercise is really a supply question. Two moves: buy *capacity* rather than parts — reserved slots, forecast-committed, called off against real demand — and push source inspection onto the supplier's floor under a delegated, audited self-certification scheme. Incoming inspection on a certified part you have already witnessed being made is theatre with a fortnight attached.

**Queue between operations.** Little's Law is unglamorous and undefeated: lead time equals work-in-process divided by throughput. If the shop holds four weeks of WIP, orders wait four weeks, and no amount of urgency changes it — expediting only reorders the queue, which is why the hot list moves individual orders and never moves the average. Cap released work. Halve WIP and you halve queue, with no capital, no headcount, and no permission required from anyone. Throughput will *rise* rather than fall, which nobody believes until they see it, and the reason nobody believes it is that Production is measured on utilisation and absorption, so idle capacity reads as failure. That's not an operations problem. That's an accounting policy generating a fourteen-week lead time.

**The end.** Documentation dossier assembly, final certification, release paperwork, shipping consolidation. Frequently a week, frequently on completed product, frequently because the dossier is compiled at the end rather than accumulated along the way.

## The move that gets to six weeks, if six weeks is even the right target

Compression of the above gets you meaningfully under ten. Getting to six is a different kind of decision, and it isn't an operations decision at all.

**Stop quoting one number.** A single lead time across a heterogeneous order book means every customer is quoted the worst case in the portfolio, and the standard configurations — which I'd wager are 60-70% of units and a smaller share of the engineering argument — are subsidising the bespoke ones with their delivery dates. Segment the catalogue. Hold semi-finished inventory at a deliberate decoupling point: common platform built to stock, differentiation applied late, final certification performed on the configured unit. Late configuration doesn't compromise certification; it *relocates* it, and where the standard permits it, that relocation is worth six weeks on its own.

Then quote 5 weeks on the standard family, 12 on engineered-to-order, and price the difference. The third of deals lost on delivery speed will not be evenly distributed across those two families, and I'd be surprised if it isn't concentrated almost entirely in the first.

## Two things I'd want tested before committing, because they may dissolve the problem

*The loss reason.* "One in three lost on delivery speed alone" is self-reported by the person who lost the deal, and delivery is the only available cause that is nobody's fault in the room. I'd want those losses reconstructed from the customer's side — thirty calls, made by someone who isn't the account manager. My expectation is that a real signal exists and is roughly half the claimed size, and that price and quoted *reliability* are hiding inside it. Which matters, because if we quote 14 and deliver 16, then nothing we do to the 14 will be believed. A credible 8 outsells an aspirational 6, and on-time-in-full is cheaper to buy than speed.

*The warranty spike itself.* Has anyone actually gone back to the failure data? Same period, same plant: overtime hours, new-hire ratio, a supplier switch, a design change, a batch of material. If the mechanism turns out to be traceable to something other than the compression, then this organisation has been governed for two years by a lesson it never verified, and the cost of that misattribution is a hundred-week lead time and one in three deals. Worth six weeks of somebody's time, I'd have thought.

## The three functions

They aren't feuding. They're each behaving correctly under the metric they were given, and the metrics are in opposition.

Sales is paid on bookings, so it promises dates it doesn't control. Production is measured on utilisation and absorption, so it batches, builds ahead, and fills the shop with the WIP that creates the queue. Quality is measured on escapes, so it adds checks and has no reason on earth to care about latency. Every one of them is being rational. Put those three people in a room and you don't get a solution, you get an accurate account of the incentive design.

So I'd change three things and not bother with the workshop.

**One shared number, on all three scorecards, at equal weight:** on-time-in-full against the quoted date, first-pass yield, warranty cost per unit shipped. Not one each. All three on all three. Sales cannot win on a promise Production can't hold; Production cannot win by shipping what comes back; Quality cannot win by making the date impossible.

**Quality gets a written, unconditional stop authority, and gets it publicly.** This looks like a concession and is in fact the enabling condition for the whole plan. Speed is only safe where someone credible can halt it, and Quality will not release latency until it is certain that integrity isn't the real target. Give that away first, in writing, before asking for anything.

**One value stream, one pilot, one tripwire.** Pick the standard family. Small co-located team, seconded not committed, with a warranty and escape-rate threshold agreed *in advance* that automatically reverts the changes if crossed. Say out loud that we expect to trip it at least once. An improvement programme that cannot fail visibly and cheaply is one that will fail invisibly and expensively, and this organisation has already had that version.

Fourteen weeks took years to accumulate and nobody chose it. It's the residue of an accounting convention, an unread archive, and one badly diagnosed failure. I'd want the first three weeks spent reading the dossiers before anybody proposes an initiative — and I'd hold the target open until we've seen the bar charts, because the number the customer is really buying may not be six.
